questions.stem: Study {figure} and answer the following questions.

parts.text: Name the computer organization shown in the figure and state its two key principles.
parts.answer: Von Neumann architecture. Instructions and data are stored in the same memory, and the CPU executes instructions sequentially unless a branch changes the control flow.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Explain the function of the control unit and the arithmetic logic unit in this organization.
parts.answer: The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and generates the control signals. The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations and records status flags.
parts.label: b

questions.stem: The CPU contains a control unit and an arithmetic logic unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the function of the control unit.
parts.answer: It fetches and decodes instructions and generates control signals that coordinate the datapath and other components.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the function of the ALU.
parts.answer: It performs arithmetic and logical operations on operands and records status flags such as zero, carry, overflow and sign.

questions.stem: Study {figure} and answer the following questions.

parts.text: Identify the register that holds the address of the next instruction and the register that holds the instruction currently being decoded.
parts.answer: PC holds the address of the next instruction; IR holds the instruction currently being decoded.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Explain the roles of MAR and MBR during a memory read.
parts.answer: The MAR holds the address to be accessed. The memory places the selected word in the MBR, which then supplies it to the CPU (for example, to the IR).
parts.label: b

parts.text: Describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle using the components shown in the figure.
parts.answer: Fetch: PC -> MAR; memory read; MBR -> IR; PC is incremented. Decode: the CU interprets the opcode in IR and issues control signals. Execute: operands are read, the ALU performs the operation, the result and flags are written back, and the next instruction is fetched.
parts.label: c

figure.caption: CPU, memory and system bus organization.

questions.stem: Study {figure} and answer the following questions.

parts.text: The cache uses a 16-bit address split into a 4-bit tag, a 3-bit line number and a 9-bit offset. For address 0x1A2B, give the tag, line number and offset in binary.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Using the cache state shown in the figure, determine whether each address is a hit or a miss: (i) 0x1A2B, (ii) 0x2A2B. Explain your reasoning.
parts.answer: (i) Hit: tag 0001 and line 101; line 5 is valid with tag 0001. (ii) Miss: tag 0010 and line 101; line 5 is valid but its tag is 0001, so the tags do not match.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Explain why the cache compares tags and how temporal and spatial locality improve the hit rate.
parts.answer: The tag identifies which memory block occupies a line; comparing tags prevents returning data from a different block. Temporal locality means recently used data is likely reused, and spatial locality means nearby addresses are likely used, so keeping blocks in cache raises the hit rate.
parts.label: c

questions.stem: The CPU can use programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O or DMA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe programmed I/O.
parts.answer: The CPU repeatedly checks the device status and transfers data itself, so it wastes time polling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe interrupt-driven I/O.
parts.answer: The device signals the CPU with an interrupt when it is ready; the CPU services the device in an ISR instead of polling.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how DMA improves I/O performance and state ONE advantage over interrupt-driven I/O.
parts.answer: A DMA controller transfers a block directly between the device and memory while the CPU continues other work; one interrupt is needed at completion, so there is less CPU overhead per transfer.

questions.stem: Interrupts can be maskable or non-maskable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Differentiate maskable and non-maskable interrupts.
parts.answer: Maskable interrupts can be disabled/delayed by the CPU; non-maskable interrupts cannot be ignored and are used for critical events.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what an interrupt handler (ISR) does.
parts.answer: It saves context, identifies the device/cause, services the request, clears the interrupt and restores context.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe TWO methods for handling multiple interrupts.
parts.answer: Priority-based nesting and polling/sequential service; nested interrupts allow a higher-priority request to pre-empt a lower-priority ISR.

questions.stem: Multicore processors are common in modern computers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define multicore processing.
parts.answer: A single processor package contains multiple independent cores that can execute instructions concurrently.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain TWO benefits of multicore processing.
parts.answer: Higher throughput on parallel workloads and better performance per watt; it can also improve responsiveness by running tasks concurrently.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe NUMA and ONE challenge in a distributed-memory system.
parts.answer: NUMA: memory access time depends on which node owns the data. Challenge: inter-node communication/synchronisation overhead and programming complexity.

questions.stem: Write appropriate programs using zero-, one- and three-address instructions to compute Z = (A - B) * C + D / E. Registers A, B, C, D and E must not be modified; X, Y and Z are temporary registers; the final answer must be stored in Z. Available instructions: zero-address PUSH, POP, ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV; one-address LOAD, STORE, ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV; three-address ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a zero-address program for the expression.
parts.answer:
PUSH A
PUSH B
SUB
PUSH C
MUL
PUSH D
PUSH E
DIV
ADD
POP Z

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a one-address program for the expression.
parts.answer:
LOAD A
SUB B
STORE X
LOAD X
MUL C
STORE X
LOAD D
DIV E
ADD X
STORE Z

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a three-address program for the expression.
parts.answer:
SUB X, A, B
MUL X, X, C
DIV Y, D, E
ADD Z, X, Y
